title: MB7-01250
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: The appellant, XXXX XXXX, a citizen of Tunisia, presented evidence before the Refugee Protection Division1 (RPD) and stated the following: - On XXXX XXXX, 2016, while with a boyfriend, he was arrested and taken to the local police station; the police laughed at them, saying they had caught faggots. They were put in a cell and were told that they would be sent to prison for public disorder. - In XXXX 2016, police officers went to his home and told his mother that there was a warrant for his arrest. - The following day, his mother went to the court house and printed out the 15-day sentence for public disorder that he received in XXXX 2016. - In his country, he was always discreet and hid his sexuality, but when he was caught or discovered by his classmates or the police, he was subjected to all kinds of humiliation. - In XXXX 2012, he was also caught with a boyfriend on a beach. He was insulted, beaten, then taken to the station, where he was humiliated all night and released the next day.2

In its decision, the RPD noted that there were omissions and contradictions, was of the opinion that the appellant's testimony was vague and hesitant and that his behaviour was inconsistent with that of an individual who fears for his life, and found that he lacked overall credibility. In summary, the RPD did not believe that he is homosexual or that he was convicted in Tunisia because of his behaviour connected to his sexual orientation.3

The appellant submits that the RPD erred in its assessment of his credibility, did not take into consideration Guidelines No. 9 of the Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) and erred by failing to consider all the evidence.4 THE REFUGEE APPEAL DIVISION (RAD)
Despite taking into consideration the Chairperson's Guideline 95 and the UNHCR's Guideline No. 9,6 I conclude that the RPD did not err. My reasons follow.

The RAD reviews RPD decisions using the correctness standard of review after conducting its own analysis of the record. The exception to this rule is when the RPD enjoys a meaningful advantage in assessing credibility.7 That said, the RAD's role is not to carry out a de novo consideration of refugee protection claims, but rather to determine whether the RPD erred, as alleged by appellants.8 Having applied that standard of review, listened to the recording of the RPD hearing9 and assessed the evidence filed before it,10 I conclude that the appellant's arguments are unfounded.

The gender identity or sexual orientation of a person claiming refugee protection is a fundamental aspect of human identity and must be addressed with sensitivity and rigour. Of course, the RPD may conclude that an individual who claims to be homosexual is not credible, but it cannot reach such a conclusion without considering all the evidence, including that individual's statements that that is indeed their sexual orientation. During a hearing, it is important to avoid perpetuating stereotypes, to ask relevant questions with sensitivity and to maintain an understanding attitude overall, not only toward sexual practices as such, but also toward society's disapproval of appearances, attitudes or behaviours deemed to be inconsistent with a society's cultural norms and values.11

On each of these points, although the RPD did not refer to the UNHCR's Guidelines No. 9 or the Chairperson's Guideline 9, it did not perpetuate stereotypes; it asked questions respectfully although, at times, it did ask the appellant to respond directly to its questions; and it gave him the opportunity to testify about his sexual orientation and the disapproval of Tunisian society toward homosexuality.12

That said, the onus is on the refugee protection claimant to establish, on a balance of probabilities, the facts on which their refugee protection claim is based, including their sexual orientation.13

Having conducted an independent assessment of all the evidence, I am of the opinion, as was the RPD, that the appellant's testimony was vague at times, notably with respect to the romantic relationships he allegedly had14 and with respect to the fact that he has allegedly had intimate sexual relations with only one man in his life, in 2008.15

I am of the opinion that the appellant failed to include relevant information in his BOC Form, particularly with respect to the names of individuals with whom he allegedly had a romantic relationship in his country as well as the death threats he received from police officers.16

And I am of the opinion that there are contradictions between his BOC Form and his testimony in terms of the problems he was facing from people other than the police in Tunisia as a result of his homosexuality.17

Moreover, I agree with the RPD's analysis to the effect that the appellant's behaviour was inconsistent with that of an individual who fears persecution in his country, given that he made several trips to Europe but did not seek asylum and that, once he arrived in Canada, he waited approximately eight months before filing a refugee protection claim.18 His explanations on this point are unreasonable.19

As for the document the appellant filed into evidence related to his conviction,20 there is nothing in the document to establish that the circumstances of that incident are connected to his homosexuality. On this point, I again agree with the RPD's analysis,21 as I have listened carefully to the appellant's testimony on this topic and concluded that it is appropriate to question why he did never made an effort to verify what was happening with his indictment once he was released from the police station in XXXX 2016.22

Finally, the appellant's criticism that the RPD did not take into consideration all of the evidence, notably the letter from his brother, is unfounded. In its reasons for decision, the RPD clearly referred to this document as well as the medical certificate.23 Having found that the appellant lacked credibility, it was open to the panel RPD to not attach any probative value to a document that simply repeated facts that it had found lacked credibility,24 given that there was no independent, credible documentary evidence on the record capable of supporting a decision in the claimant's favour.25 CONCLUSION
For these reasons, I confirm the RPD determination, namely that XXXX XXXX is neither a refugee under section 96 of the IRPA nor a person in need of protection under section 97 of the same act.

The appeal is dismissed.
